header: // The AI turn: rate limits, context assembly, the streaming reply loop with
// throttled edit-in-place, reaction handling, memory consolidation and error
// surfacing. This is the single most performance-sensitive path in the bot —
// it runs inside the queue consumer, never inside the webhook request.
// Button taps: menu navigation and the full admin/self-service callback
// surface. Bundled as one unit because the dispatch switch and the shared
// helpers it uses are tightly coupled and split apart would only add
// indirection.
// Webhook fast path: decides whether an update can skip the queue entirely.
// Incoming message pipeline: group access checks, flow-state interception
// (setup wizards own the next message), command dispatch, and the group
// trigger / reaction logic that decides whether Nyra answers at all.
// Command parsing: `/cmd@BotName arg1 arg2` -> { command, args }, honouring
// the bot's own @username so a command addressed to a different bot in the
// same group is ignored rather than executed.
// POST /webhook. This is the durability boundary: the update is
// deduplicated by update_id and enqueued *before* the 200, so a Telegram
// retry never double-processes and a failed enqueue releases the dedup slot.
// GET /status — plain-text status and bootstrap endpoint. The Mini App owns
// "/", so this is the URL that initialises the schema, teaches the Worker
// its public origin, and registers the Telegram webhook + menu button.
// GET /setup?url= — manual webhook (re)registration, authenticated with the
// same derived secret Telegram uses. Refuses secrets in the query string.
// Kept because it is the escape hatch when automatic discovery is wrong.

barrelHeader: // `src/index.js` imports from here; the Worker's `export default { fetch,
// scheduled, queue }` stays in src/index.js because that is the composition
// root binding these handlers to the runtime.
